claims.text: The as-synthesized selected high-entropy alloy has high configurational or atomic disorder.
The as-synthesized selected alloy has no superconducting transition or only very weak superconducting signatures.
Controlled thermal annealing can reduce atomic disorder and promote local chemical ordering in the selected alloy.
Annealing under an inert atmosphere can produce ordering without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Suitable annealing parameters can modify disorder while retaining the high-entropy alloy phase and avoiding phase segregation.
Sharper X-ray diffraction peaks would evidence enhanced local chemical ordering and reduced atomic-scale disorder.
Transmission electron microscopy can provide evidence of enhanced local structural or chemical ordering.
Reducing configurational disorder improves local electron-phonon coupling in the selected alloy.
The improved electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation.
Annealing-induced ordering will produce superconductivity that is absent or weak in the highly disordered starting state.
Annealed samples will have a higher critical temperature than the as-synthesized baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a narrower superconducting transition than the as-synthesized baseline.
Superconducting transitions near or below 10 K are a relevant test regime for high-entropy superconductors.
The proposed relationship should hold only while annealing modestly improves ordering without causing deleterious phase separation.
Chemical-pressure effects could alternatively contribute to changes in superconducting behavior.
If increased local ordering is the driver, it should occur concomitantly with an increased critical temperature and a sharper superconducting transition.
Failure to observe reproducible concomitant enhancement of ordering, critical temperature, and transition sharpness relative to the untreated control is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
